items.stemHtml:
A 38-year-old woman has vomited repeatedly for 6 days from gastric outlet obstruction. She is lightheaded on standing. Laboratory studies:

TestResult
Sodium133 mEq/L
Potassium2.7 mEq/L
Chloride80 mEq/L
Bicarbonate38 mEq/L
pH7.52
PaCO248 mmHg
Urine pH5.5
Urine chloride8 mEq/L

Which of the following best explains why her urine is acidic despite systemic alkalemia?

options.label: B
options.html: Chloride depletion stimulating proximal bicarbonate secretion

options.label: C
options.html: Hypokalemia suppressing distal hydrogen ion secretion

options.label: D
options.html: Respiratory compensation acidifying the tubular fluid

options.label: E
options.html: Volume and chloride depletion driving distal H⁺ secretion

items.explanationHtml:
Vomiting removes HCl and generates the alkalosis; the kidney maintains it. Volume depletion activates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, and chloride depletion means sodium cannot be reabsorbed with chloride. The kidney therefore reabsorbs sodium distally in exchange for hydrogen and potassium ions (aldosterone stimulates the α-intercalated H⁺-ATPase and principal-cell ENaC). Hypokalemia adds to H⁺ secretion and ammoniagenesis. The result is paradoxical aciduria, which persists until saline and potassium chloride are given.

Takeaway: in chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis, volume and chloride depletion make the distal nephron secrete H⁺, so urine is paradoxically acidic until saline and KCl are given.

whyNot.A: Stool bicarbonate loss causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, the opposite disorder.
whyNot.B: Chloride depletion impairs bicarbonate secretion by β-intercalated cells (pendrin), which is part of why the alkalosis is maintained; it does not acidify urine.
whyNot.C: Volume depletion raises aldosterone; hypokalemia slightly lowers aldosterone but increases H⁺ secretion and ammonium production.
whyNot.D: Respiratory compensation raises PaCO₂ but the blood remains alkalemic; it does not explain an acidic urine.

items.objective: Explain paradoxical aciduria in vomiting-induced metabolic alkalosis.
